c1-m1.summary: The user has fond memories of frequenting Jonathan's with their family.
c1-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hi, I was just thinking about my favorite childhood restaurants. Do you think it's common for people to have a special place they like to go back to?
Assistant: Yes, I think it's very common. Many people have fond memories of certain restaurants that they visited frequently when they were young. It's often a combination of the food, atmosphere, and nostalgia that makes them special.
User: That makes sense. I think the atmosphere and nostalgia play a big role in it. Some places just feel like home, you know?
Assistant: Absolutely. It's as if the restaurant becomes a part of your family's tradition and history. What kind of restaurants do you usually think of when you think of your childhood?
User: Hmm, I guess I think of casual, family-friendly places. You know, the kind of place where you can just relax and be yourself.
Assistant: Those are the best kind of places. No fuss, no frills, just good food and good company. Did you have a specific restaurant in mind when you were thinking about this?
User: Yeah, I did. But it's funny, I haven't thought about it in years. I guess it's just been on my mind lately.
Assistant: It's interesting how memories can resurface like that. Sometimes it's just a smell or a taste that can bring back a flood of memories. Do you think you'll ever go back to this restaurant?
User: I'm not even sure if it's still open. But I think I might have to look it up and see. It would be nice to relive some of those memories.
Assistant: That sounds like a great idea. Even if it's not the same as it was when you were a kid, it's still a way to connect with your past and recapture some of that nostalgia.
User: Yeah, I think you're right. You know, this person... actually, it was me... has fond memories of frequenting Jonathan's with my family.
Assistant: Ah, Jonathan's! So that's the restaurant that's been on your mind. What was it about Jonathan's that made it so special for you and your family?
User: Well, the food was always great, but it was more than that. The owners knew us by name, and we always felt welcome. It was just a really warm and inviting place to be.
Assistant: That sounds wonderful. It's clear that Jonathan's was more than just a restaurant to you and your family. It was a gathering place, a spot where you could connect with each other and with the community.
User: Exactly. And I think that's what I miss about it the most. It's not just the food or the atmosphere, but the sense of connection and belonging that came with it.
Assistant: I think that's what makes Jonathan's such a special place in your memories. It's not just a restaurant, but a symbol of the time you spent with your family and the memories you created together.
User: Hi, I'm looking for some recommendations for restaurants. I'm really craving something good today.
Assistant: I'd be happy to help you with some recommendations. What kind of cuisine are you in the mood for?
User: Hmm, that's a tough one. I think I'd love some Italian food. Do you have any suggestions?
Assistant: Italian sounds great! There are many excellent Italian restaurants. Can you tell me a bit more about what you're looking for? Are you looking for something fancy or more casual?
User: Casual is fine, I just want something that tastes good. Do you have any specific recommendations?
Assistant: Well, there's a great Italian place that's highly rated. It's called Bella Vita. Have you heard of it?
User: Actually, yes, I have. I used to go there all the time. But I'm not sure if it's still good.
Assistant: It's still getting great reviews. But if you're looking for something new, I can suggest a few other options. What did you like about Bella Vita?
User: The pasta dishes were amazing, and the service was always friendly. I really loved the atmosphere too.
Assistant: That sounds wonderful. I think you might be happy to know that they still have a great selection of pasta dishes. But I have to ask, why did you stop going there?
User: Well... I don't live in the area anymore.
Assistant: Oh, I see. Did you move to a different part of the city?
User: Actually, I moved to a different country for work and am no longer in the vicinity of the restaurant.
Assistant: That's a big change. I can imagine you must miss your favorite restaurants. Do you think you'll ever be back in the area to visit Bella Vita again?
User: I hope so, but it's hard to say. I'd love to go back and try some of their new dishes. Maybe someday I'll be back in the area for work or a visit.
Assistant: Well, I hope that happens for you. In the meantime, I can try to help you find a similar Italian restaurant in your new location. Would you like that?

c13-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Write a fictional story of approximately 1500-2000 words, using a third-person limited point of view, centered around a chef named Jonathan who decides to start his own cooking school after years of working in the restaurant industry. The story should focus on Jonathan's journey as he navigates the challenges of starting a new business and the personal growth he experiences as he becomes more of a mentor to his students. Be sure to include details about the types of classes Jonathan teaches, the personalities and backgrounds of some of his students, and the different obstacles he faces along the way. In addition, use descriptive language and sensory details to help bring the setting and characters to life for the reader.
Assistant: Jonathan had always been passionate about food. From a young age, he had found solace in the kitchen, experimenting with different ingredients and flavors to create mouth-watering meals that his family and friends couldn't resist. It was no surprise, then, that he ended up pursuing a career in the restaurant industry; working as a chef in some of the finest kitchens across the country.

Despite his success in the industry, Jonathan had always felt that something was missing. He loved cooking, of course, but he wanted to do more than just create delicious meals for customers. He wanted to share his knowledge and expertise with others; to inspire budding chefs to hone their skills and pursue their own culinary dreams. And so, after years of contemplation, Jonathan decided to take the leap and start his own cooking school.

It wasn't an easy decision. Jonathan knew that starting a business was far from easy, especially in the competitive world of cooking schools. But he was determined to make it work, and so he began putting together a plan, researching different teaching methods, and reaching out to potential students.

The first challenge was finding the right location. Jonathan wanted a space that was big enough to accommodate a kitchen, a dining area, and a classroom, but wasn't so large that it would be financially draining. After weeks of searching, he finally found a small, cozy space in the heart of the city that fit the bill. It needed some work, of course - the walls were drab, the floors were scuffed, and the kitchen needed a complete overhaul - but Jonathan saw the potential.

Over the course of several months, Jonathan worked tirelessly to transform the space into a beautiful, functional cooking school. The reviews of the book led me to expect something with the page-turning qualities of a good murder mystery combined with an unusual, and more poetic, use of language than you generally find in genre fiction. The book seemed to live up to that description for the first fifty pages or so, but I seriously question whether many reviewers read the entire novel, because by the middle the plot bogs down, it becomes clear that the characters are never going to develop into anything more complicated than you'd find in a B movie, and the language, at first intriguing, becomes just plain eccentric. Assistant: That's a great idea, Neighbors A. You always have such a good eye for capturing the moment.
User: Thanks, I just love looking back on old pictures and remembering all the good times we've had together.
Assistant: Speaking of good times, do you remember that time when we got lost in the woods and you were such a great leader?
User: Oh yeah, that was a scary experience. But I'm glad I could help you out and build that shelter for us.
Assistant: It just goes to show that you have so many talents, Neighbors A. Remember when you started fixing things around the house and in the garage?
User: Of course, that was a couple of years ago now. But I'm still enjoying working on projects and feeling more confident in my skills.
Assistant: That's great to hear, Neighbors A. You really have a lot to offer and I'm glad we're friends.
User: Did you hear about Jonathan's dedication to making the school baseball team?
Assistant: No, I haven't. What did he do?
User: Apparently, he took an hour of batting practice every day and another hour to work on his pitching skills.
Assistant: Wow, that's really impressive. Did it pay off?
User: It sure did! He made the team and even got a starting position.
Assistant: That's great! I remember when I played baseball in high school. It took a lot of hard work to make the team too.
User: Definitely. It's important to put in the effort and dedication if you want to achieve your goals.
Assistant: Absolutely. It reminds me of when I was trying to make the basketball team. I would practice every day, and it paid off when I made the team.
User: That's awesome! I think it's important to have that kind of drive and determination, no matter what your goals are.

c33-m1.summary: The assistant helped the user find the tools in the garage.
c33-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Did you find the tools in the garage?
Assistant: Yes, thanks to Jonathan's honesty. He told me they were on the left side, behind the door.
User: Jonathan is always honest. He never holds back the truth, no matter how difficult it is.
Assistant: That's true. I've always admired his integrity.
User: Remember when he returned that wallet he found on the school bus?
Assistant: Yes, he could have easily kept it, but he chose to do the right thing. He even made sure the owner got it back.
User: It's refreshing to have someone like Jonathan in our class. He sets a good example for all of us.
Assistant: Definitely. I hope we can all learn from his honesty and integrity.
User: Hey, Neighbor B! How are you doing today?
Assistant: I'm doing good, thanks. How about you?
User: I'm feeling grateful today. I've been thinking about the time we spent together a few weeks ago. It was a really special moment for me, and I just wanted to let you know how much I appreciated it.
Assistant: Aw, that's really sweet of you to say. What moment are you referring to exactly?
User: You know, when we went for that walk in the park and talked about how we both enjoy volunteering. I felt like we really connected over our shared values.
Assistant: Oh yeah, I remember that. It was nice to have someone to talk to who understands the importance of giving back to the community.
User: Definitely. And speaking of community, I wanted to tell you about something else that's been on my mind lately. As you know, I rent out an apartment to tenants, and I've been thinking about ways to make sure the building is a positive presence in the neighborhood.
Assistant: That's a good mindset to have. What kind of ideas are you considering?
User: Well, for starters, I want to make sure the building is well-maintained and doesn't become an eyesore for the community. But beyond that, I think there are opportunities to get involved in local events or programs that benefit the area.
Assistant: That sounds like a great idea. It's always nice when landlords take an active interest in the well-being of their tenants and the community as a whole.
User: I agree. And on a completely different note, I also wanted to share with you that my work at the stock exchange has been going really well lately. I'm proud of the progress I've made and the success I've had helping clients make smart investments.
Assistant: Congratulations, that's great to hear! It's always inspiring to see someone excel at what they do.
User: Thank you, I really appreciate that. So, have you been up to anything interesting lately?
Assistant: Not really, just trying to stay busy with work and some hobbies I enjoy. But I'm hoping to take a trip somewhere soon, if I can find the time and funds to do it.
User: That sounds like a great idea. Traveling is one of my favorite ways to take a break from the daily grind and recharge my batteries.
Assistant: Yeah, it's always nice to get a change of scenery and experience new things. Maybe we can swap travel stories sometime.
User: Definitely, I'd love that. Thanks for chatting, Neighbor B. Have a great day!
Assistant: You too, Neighbor A. See you later!

c35-m1.summary: Hodinkee started as a Tumblr page by Ben Clymer, who was passionate about mechanical watches.
c35-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Given the text: He’s lived and studied in three culturally-diverse countries. Now, Jonathan’s using his cultural powers to enhance his impact as a Resident Leader (RL).
Originally from Hong Kong, Jonathan moved halfway around the world to complete high school in the United Kingdom.
“After high school, I wanted to study Physiotherapy at Birmingham University,” Jonathan said.
Jonathan may not have stepped so easily into higher education, but he has stayed true to his initial career ambitions, taking on a Bachelor of Exercise and Sports Science.
Since moving to Darwin, though, Jonathan has had to adjust to the local pace and attitude. He’s also learnt new ways of keeping himself motivated in a relaxed environment.
“A challenging aspect here is probably self-discipline,” Jonathan said. “Life is busy in Hong Kong; everything has a schedule and is packed full. Before you finish the work you are doing, you already need to be thinking about the next thing you need to do."
For a lover of all things physical, it makes sense for Jonathan to look to NBA star Derrick Rose for inspiration during the lows of motivation.
Being an RL at IHD isn’t the first time Jonathan’s experienced such a role, and it’s made his interpersonal skills a valuable asset to the team.

Question/Instruction: How have economic and aesthetic factors contributed to the trend towards renovating and preserving older buildings rather than starting from scratch?

Given material: THE VERY IDEA OF a face lift goes against the grain of most architects' thinking. Their instincts lean much more toward all-out plastic surgery, reshaping the body to take on a whole different cast. That is, if they are willing to keep the old body at all. Throwing it out and starting from scratch probably gets closer to their way of doing things.
Architects, so the common wisdom goes, want to remake the world, or at least as much of it as they can get their hands on. It's been true enough in the past, but has become less and less so in the last decade, as the architectural profession has been forced to face twin realities: the growing preference in our society both for preserving older buildings and for renovating what we have, rather than starting over again. Renovation is usually, though not always, cheaper than new construction, which makes it especially appealing in an age of monetary constraints. So it is partly a matter of esthetics, partly economics and partly common sense that have brought us here. But we are clearly at a moment when few architects dare to treat a renovation project as if it were a blank slate.
A generation ago, architects were taught that their mission was to leave a mark, and often, the stronger the better. New buildings were designed to stand out from their surroundings; renovations of older ones were done so that no one could fail to see the difference between the original and the addition. Even architects whose careers began relatively recently tended to operate this way. Think, for example, of Michael Graves, the Princeton, N.J.-based architect who in the late 1960's and early 70's first came into public view through the striking modernist additions he put onto older houses (which led some colleagues to dub him the ''Cubist kitchen king''). The very point of Graves's additions was to stand apart from the houses to which they were attached. They were highly abstract objects, possessed of far more sophistication than the original houses, and their aloofness was part of the architectural message. ''You are common, but I am something much more special,'' the additions seemed to sneer at the houses.
The attitude of Graves's early years was hardly his alone. At the beginning of the 70's, the New York City firm of Mayers & Schiff designed an addition to an old clapboard farmhouse in Connecticut in the form of a two-story-high cedar and glass box. Lest there be any mistake about the transition from new to old, the box was set at a diagonal from the original house and wrapped around one of its corners, the new literally encasing the old.
Even Robert A. M. Stern, an architect whose career has soared in the last decade, largely due to his success in reproducing traditional architectural styles, nonetheless felt that he could not afford to let his own work disappear beside that of another architect. At least that is what one major addition he completed in 1981 would suggest. The house is a huge Georgian-style mansion in Llewelyn Park, N.J.; the addition, which contains an indoor pool, is best described as something of an English Baroque pleasure pavilion with a greenhouse roof. And while it picks up a few details from the original house, no one could say it blends in softly.
IT IS TEMPTING TO think of the whole issue in terms of ego, given how much, even today, our image of the architect is shaped by such fictitious characters as Howard Roark in the Ayn Rand novel ''The Fountainhead.'' Her architect-hero stands defiantly against bourgeois taste, and would sooner burn his T-square than design a building that took its cues from anyone else's. But for all we might want to see the architect as a romantic hero - for all architects might want to see themselves as such - the truth is that most architecture is shaped by the prevailing taste of an age.
As a matter of fact, ego has relatively little to do with it. Indeed, in recent years some of the biggest egos in architecture have begun to do some of the most restrained work. Kevin Roche, who gave us the monumental additions to The Metropolitan Museum of Art in the 70's - wings whose glass and limestone forms contrast sharply with the classical, older sections of the Met - recently designed an addition to the Jewish Museum on Fifth Avenue that is simply an exact reproduction of the museum's original French Gothic mansion. The addition, which will go into construction later this year, is conceived as if to blend new and old into a seamless whole.
Similarly, Romaldo Giurgola, a winner of the American Institute of Architects' highest award, has proposed adding to Louis I. Kahn's Kimbell Museum of Art in Fort Worth by literally extending its design at each end. That project hasn't been received as well as the Roche plan, largely because the Kimbell, unlike the Jewish Museum, is considered to be one of the great works of American architecture. Tampering with it at all, even by replicating the original, has been viewed by many critics as akin to adding a few strokes to a Caravaggio.
These two examples are extreme ones, of course. Precisely duplicating what has come before is hardly the only mode of the hour, particularly for public buildings. But it is being done more and more. And the fact that architects of Giurgola's stature, or Roche's, would consider replicating sections of older buildings tells us how much architectural values have changed.
In the last few years, there has been less hubris in architectural design, less of the arrogant certainty that we can do much better than the architects of earlier generations, and much less of the patronizing attitude toward tradition that for many architects was the motivation for breaking away from the old style when designing a renovation or addition. The original building was there first - a simple fact, but one that today has come to earn it a certain degree of respect. We do not condescend to Georgian or Tudor or Shingle Style houses the way we once did. And we are much more likely now to understand how good the average, traditionally styled American house built before 1940 really is. Architects today know better than to treat it with scorn.
MORE THAN INSISTENT originality, we seek a kind of wholeness now, a sense that a building is part of a larger continuity. And if that means the architect is going to be able to express his or her own design sensibility slightly less, we seem to feel that it is a fair trade-off. By the same token, an expanded or renovated house need not look merely like a bigger version of what was there before. But it should take its cues from the original building. Sometimes those cues can be interpreted literally; in other circumstances, it makes more sense to let the original building set a tone, a direction to which the second architect can respond. Inside, the rooms were reorganized to flow gracefully into one another. The result, which was finished in 1987, is a lively and energetic composition that manages not to be overrefined or precious. It's been true enough in the past, but has become less and less so in the last decade, as the architectural profession has been forced to face twin realities: the growing preference in our society both for preserving older buildings and for renovating what we have, rather than starting over again. Renovation is usually, though not always, cheaper than new construction, which makes it especially appealing in an age of monetary constraints. So it is partly a matter of esthetics, partly economics and partly common sense that have brought us here. But we are clearly at a moment when few architects dare to treat a renovation project as if it were a blank slate.
A generation ago, architects were taught that their mission was to leave a mark, and often, the stronger the better. New buildings were designed to stand out from their surroundings; renovations of older ones were done so that no one could fail to see the difference between the original and the addition. Even architects whose careers began relatively recently tended to operate this way. Think, for example, of Michael Graves, the Princeton, N.J.-based architect who in the late 1960's and early 70's first came into public view through the striking modernist additions he put onto older houses (which led some colleagues to dub him the ''Cubist kitchen king''). The very point of Graves's additions was to stand apart from the houses to which they were attached. They were highly abstract objects, possessed of far more sophistication than the original houses, and their aloofness was part of the architectural message. ''You are common, but I am something much more special,'' the additions seemed to sneer at the houses.
The attitude of Graves's early years was hardly his alone. At the beginning of the 70's, the New York City firm of Mayers & Schiff designed an addition to an old clapboard farmhouse in Connecticut in the form of a two-story-high cedar and glass box. Lest there be any mistake about the transition from new to old, the box was set at a diagonal from the original house and wrapped around one of its corners, the new literally encasing the old.
Even Robert A. M. Stern, an architect whose career has soared in the last decade, largely due to his success in reproducing traditional architectural styles, nonetheless felt that he could not afford to let his own work disappear beside that of another architect. At least that is what one major addition he completed in 1981 would suggest. The house is a huge Georgian-style mansion in Llewelyn Park, N.J.; the addition, which contains an indoor pool, is best described as something of an English Baroque pleasure pavilion with a greenhouse roof. And while it picks up a few details from the original house, no one could say it blends in softly.
IT IS TEMPTING TO think of the whole issue in terms of ego, given how much, even today, our image of the architect is shaped by such fictitious characters as Howard Roark in the Ayn Rand novel ''The Fountainhead.'' Her architect-hero stands defiantly against bourgeois taste, and would sooner burn his T-square than design a building that took its cues from anyone else's. But for all we might want to see the architect as a romantic hero - for all architects might want to see themselves as such - the truth is that most architecture is shaped by the prevailing taste of an age.
As a matter of fact, ego has relatively little to do with it. Indeed, in recent years some of the biggest egos in architecture have begun to do some of the most restrained work. Kevin Roche, who gave us the monumental additions to The Metropolitan Museum of Art in the 70's - wings whose glass and limestone forms contrast sharply with the classical, older sections of the Met - recently designed an addition to the Jewish Museum on Fifth Avenue that is simply an exact reproduction of the museum's original French Gothic mansion. The addition, which will go into construction later this year, is conceived as if to blend new and old into a seamless whole.
Similarly, Romaldo Giurgola, a winner of the American Institute of Architects' highest award, has proposed adding to Louis I. Kahn's Kimbell Museum of Art in Fort Worth by literally extending its design at each end. That project hasn't been received as well as the Roche plan, largely because the Kimbell, unlike the Jewish Museum, is considered to be one of the great works of American architecture. Tampering with it at all, even by replicating the original, has been viewed by many critics as akin to adding a few strokes to a Caravaggio.
These two examples are extreme ones, of course. Precisely duplicating what has come before is hardly the only mode of the hour, particularly for public buildings. But it is being done more and more. And the fact that architects of Giurgola's stature, or Roche's, would consider replicating sections of older buildings tells us how much architectural values have changed.
In the last few years, there has been less hubris in architectural design, less of the arrogant certainty that we can do much better than the architects of earlier generations, and much less of the patronizing attitude toward tradition that for many architects was the motivation for breaking away from the old style when designing a renovation or addition. The original building was there first - a simple fact, but one that today has come to earn it a certain degree of respect. We do not condescend to Georgian or Tudor or Shingle Style houses the way we once did. And we are much more likely now to understand how good the average, traditionally styled American house built before 1940 really is. Architects today know better than to treat it with scorn.
MORE THAN INSISTENT originality, we seek a kind of wholeness now, a sense that a building is part of a larger continuity. And if that means the architect is going to be able to express his or her own design sensibility slightly less, we seem to feel that it is a fair trade-off. By the same token, an expanded or renovated house need not look merely like a bigger version of what was there before. But it should take its cues from the original building. Sometimes those cues can be interpreted literally; in other circumstances, it makes more sense to let the original building set a tone, a direction to which the second architect can respond. If architecture can be thought of as a conversation, the new architect entering the house doesn't need to repeat the words of the first architect - but he or she at least ought to be speaking the same language.
A couple of recent examples: In Larchmont, N.Y., in 1987, the architects Karen Bausman and Leslie Gill of Bausman-Gill Associates completed a two-story modernist addition to a tiny one-story stucco cottage. To have the extra space they wanted yet still preserve several valued trees on the small plot, the addition had to be two stories tall. Had it imitated the Arts and Crafts style of the cottage, it would have risked overwhelming the original building. But the finished addition appears neither to dominate the cottage nor to be incompatible with it. Bausman-Gill used the same material, stucco, as in the original building and similar steel casement windows, allowing the cottage to initiate the conversation, so to speak. The result is a deft marriage of old and new, the whole being both comfortable and visually richer than either section could be on its own.
Similarly, the San Francisco architect Mark Mack took a less literal direction in his addition to a rough-concrete modern house of the 60's, set high in the hills of Berkeley, Calif. Mack's own work has a blunt, almost primitive quality to it, which created a certain compatibility at the outset. But the addition, completed in 1988, stands out sharply from the original building: Its stucco walls are painted a rusty red with indigo-blue trim, and it reads as a powerful sculptural presence on its own. Still, it was not built to stand alone, and doesn't. The addition and the original house strengthen each other, forming a complex and vivid whole. (Mack considered a scheme that was more literally derived from the original house, and left it up to the clients to decide how assertive they wanted him to be. He was pleased with their decision; the other scheme, he felt, was too accommodating.) While the version that was built is hardly indifferent to the original building, it strikes out independently - yet in a way that relates continually to the original, engaging it in a vibrant architectural dialogue.
The conversation is quieter on Long Island, where David Hannaford Mitchell transformed a huge white clapboard farmhouse in Remsenburg into a rambling but vastly more genteel house. The changes Mitchell made are quite dramatic. He took a bland building and refined it, adding shutters, multipaned windows, a cornice and decks framed in subtly detailed latticework. Inside, the rooms were reorganized to flow gracefully into one another. The result, which was finished in 1987, is a lively and energetic composition that manages not to be overrefined or precious. The basic strength of the big old farmhouse is still there: It has been dressed up on the outside and opened up inside to just the right degree to bring out its architectural potential.
And so it is with all of the best renovations. They do not defy or sneer at the buildings to which they are appended, but support them. Sometimes buildings are supported best simply by being continued or extended, sometimes by being altered quite dramatically. The point is that whatever is done, it is the original building that sets the tone.

The best renovations do not dominate or sneer at the original building, but support and enhance it, whether by continuing or extending it, or altering it dramatically while still responding to its language. User: Start automating security testing in four steps: drill down, context from the inside, see actionable reports, and customize your workflow.
Micro Focus WebInspect is an automated dynamic testing solution that discovers configuration issues, and identifies and prioritizes security vulnerabilities in running applications. It mimics real-world hacking techniques and provides comprehensive dynamic analysis of complex web applications and services. WebInspect dashboards and reports provide organizations with visibility and an accurate risk posture of your applications.
WebInspect enables you to observe application reaction to attacks at the code level during dynamic scans, identify and crawl more of an application to expand the coverage of the attack surface, and provide stack traces and SQL queries to confirmed vulnerabilities.
Create flexible, extensible, and scalable reports that match your business requirements. HTTP requests and responses are contextually highlighted to immediately draw attention to the attack and the vulnerable response. You can easily retest the entire site, just the vulnerabilities, or only a single vulnerability, as well as scan comparison which enables the delta analysis comparison of vulnerabilities across two scans.
Centralize your security intelligence using WebInspect Enterprise, which helps you understand the security risk of your organization. Providing you the ability to view and manage your security portfolio to track vulnerability, confirm remediation, view metrics, progress and trends.
WebInspect is an automated dynamic testing tool that mimics real-world hacking techniques and attacks, and provides comprehensive dynamic analysis of complex web applications and services.
The earlier in the development process that security vulnerabilities are discovered, the less expensive they are to fix. WebInspect gives security professionals and security novices alike the power and knowledge to quickly identify and validate critical, high-risk security vulnerabilities in applications running in development, QA, or production.
Do more with less. WebInspect improves the effectiveness of your DAST efforts while lowering the cost of security vulnerability assessment and remediation. Advanced technologies like simultaneous crawl and audit, and concurrent scanning makes powerful scanning technology accessible to even novice security testers.
Streamline the process of remediating vulnerabilities. WebInspect Enterprise establishes a shared security service to centralize and correlate results while distributing security intelligence, or testing capabilities, across an organization. Summarize the capabilities of WebInspect and explain how it can assist security professionals in identifying and validating security vulnerabilities.

It provides comprehensive dynamic analysis of complex web applications and services, enabling security professionals and novices to quickly identify and validate critical, high-risk security vulnerabilities in applications running in development, QA or production.

With WebInspect, organizations can discover configuration issues, identify and prioritize security vulnerabilities, and observe application reaction to attacks at the code level. The tool also enables you to expand the coverage of the attack surface, provide stack traces and SQL queries to confirmed vulnerabilities, and create flexible, extensible and scalable reports that match your business requirements.

WebInspect Enterprise centralizes security intelligence, enabling organizations to understand the security risk and track vulnerability, confirm remediation, view metrics, progress and trends. The shared security service also helps streamline the process of remediating vulnerabilities, making powerful scanning technology accessible to even novice security testers.

Overall, WebInspect improves the effectiveness of DAST efforts while lowering the cost of security vulnerability assessment and remediation. User: What are some examples of "radical" devices that are likely to become widespread over the next decade to help consumers make better-informed decisions about their food? Answer according to: Will Technology Change The Way We Eat?
The Food Innovation Summit held in Washington DC explored how the food technologies of tomorrow will change the way we eat.
For example - tooth sensors that measure sugar and alcohol intake and ingestible health monitors could shape the future of the food industry.
Max Elder, a researcher at the Institute for the Future's Food Futures Lab, said "the future is already here." He said that if CPGs want to prepare for future obstacles now then they will need to "work backwards" to strategize steps they can take to create the industry they want. "We do not sit in our little think tank in Palo Alto and look at our crystal balls and make some statement that in 10 years X will happen," he said. "Instead, what we can do is identify preferred futures so we can think about what we want the future to look like."
A recent study by the Center for Food Integrity also found that only 33% of survey respondents "strongly agree" that they are confident in the safety of the food they consume. Because of this distrust, a new suite of technologies has been developed to help consumers make better-informed decisions about their food, Elder said. He said these "radical" devices would likely be widespread over the next decade.
For example, a lab at Carnegie Mellon University is working to develop an ingestible sensor that would monitor gastrointestinal health.
Tufts University has created a tooth sensor, which is two millimeters by two millimeters, that can measure glucose, sugar and alcohol intake.
Baidu, a Chinese search engine plant, developed smart chopsticks that can detect the freshness of cooking oil.
Nima is a portable sensor that tests for trace amounts of gluten when users put crumbs of food in a small machine.
The future of food is upon us.
Assistant: Other examples of "radical" devices that are likely to become widespread over the next decade include:

1. Smart packaging: This technology uses sensors and other smart tools to monitor the condition of food inside the package. For example, a chip embedded in the packaging could alert consumers if the food is nearing its expiration date, or if it has been exposed to unfavorable conditions during transport.

2. Virtual reality food experiences: VR headsets and other immersive technologies may be used to create virtual restaurant experiences or to help consumers visualize their meals before they even order them.

3. Personalized nutrition plans: Using genetic testing and other advanced tools, it may become possible to create highly personalized nutrition plans that are tailored to an individual's unique needs and preferences.

4. 3D-printed food: This technology could allow for highly customized, nutrient-dense meals to be printed on demand, potentially reducing food waste and increasing efficiency in the food industry.

Overall, the integration of technology into the food industry is set to transform the way we eat, from how we shop and prepare our meals to the very nature of what we consume.
User: Can you provide more details about how the tooth sensor created by Tufts University works?
Assistant: Yes! The tooth sensor, created by Tufts University, is a tiny device that can be attached to a tooth like a dental brace or filling. It uses wireless communication to send information about a person's dietary habits to a mobile device or computer.

The sensor is powered by a small battery and can be removed or replaced, making it easy for users to switch it out when needed. It is also designed to be safe for long-term use, with biocompatible materials that won't harm the tooth or surrounding tissue.

The tooth sensor has the potential to revolutionize the way we track our dietary habits and manage our health, providing real-time feedback on our eating habits and helping us make better-informed decisions about what we eat.
User: Can you give me more information about the lab at Carnegie Mellon University that is developing an ingestible sensor to monitor gastrointestinal health?
Assistant: Sure! The lab at Carnegie Mellon University that is developing an ingestible sensor to monitor gastrointestinal health is part of the university's College of Engineering. The lab is led by Dr. Christopher Bettinger, a professor of Materials Science and Biomedical Engineering, and focuses on the development of novel biomaterials and medical devices.

The ingestible sensor that the lab is working on is designed to monitor the digestive system in real-time, allowing doctors and patients to track the progression of certain diseases and conditions. The sensor is made from a variety of materials, including biocompatible polymers and electronics that can withstand the harsh environment of the digestive system.

The device works by transmitting data wirelessly to an external device, such as a smartphone or computer, which can be used to monitor the patient's health and alert medical professionals to potential issues. The sensor is also designed to break down and pass through the body after a certain amount of time, reducing the risk of any adverse effects or complications.

The development of this technology has the potential to revolutionize the way we monitor and treat digestive disorders, providing patients with real-time feedback on their health and helping doctors make more informed decisions about their care.

c67-m1.summary: The user is planning a trip to a foreign country.
c67-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Hi, I'm thinking of traveling to a foreign country soon. Can you help me decide which one to visit?
Assistant: I'd be happy to help. What type of culture or experience are you looking for in a foreign country?
User: I'm not sure, but I've always been interested in trying new foods and drinks. Do you have any recommendations?
Assistant: Trying new cuisine is a great way to experience a culture. Countries like Japan, Italy, and Thailand are known for their unique and delicious food. But if you're also interested in drinks, you might want to consider countries like Turkey or Morocco, which have a rich tea culture.
User: That sounds great. I think I'd like to visit a country with a rich tea culture. But what if I don't speak the language?
Assistant: Don't worry, many countries cater to tourists and offer English translations. However, it's always appreciated when visitors make an effort to learn a few basic phrases in the local language.
User: I never thought of that. I think I'd like to learn a few basic phrases. Do you have any language learning tips?
Assistant: Definitely. One tip is to start with simple phrases like "hello" and "thank you." You can also try listening to music or watching TV shows in the target language to get a feel for how it sounds.
User: That's a great idea. I think I'm going to try that. By the way, I've always been fascinated by different languages. I love listening to people speak in their native tongue and trying to pick up on the nuances of the language.
Assistant: That's really cool. Being fascinated by languages can definitely enhance your travel experiences. Have you ever thought about taking a language course or attending a language exchange event?
User: Actually, I haven't, but that sounds like a great idea. Do you think it would be helpful to learn the grammar rules of a language, or should I focus more on conversational skills?
Assistant: Both are important, but if you're looking to communicate effectively with native speakers, conversational skills are key. Focus on learning common phrases and practicing your pronunciation.
User: Okay, got it. What about language learning apps? Are there any that you would recommend?
Assistant: Yes, there are many great language learning apps out there. Some popular ones include Duolingo, Babbel, and Rosetta Stone. They offer interactive lessons and exercises to help you learn a language at your own pace.
User: Great, I'll definitely check those out. Thanks for the advice!
Assistant: You're welcome. Good luck with your language learning journey, and I hope you have a great time on your travels!
User: Hi, I'm trying to learn a new language, but I'm having some trouble staying motivated. Do you have any advice?
Assistant: Staying motivated can be tough, but there are many ways to overcome that. Can you tell me a bit more about your goals and what you've been doing so far to learn the language?
User: Well, I've been using some language learning apps and trying to practice speaking with native speakers online. But I just feel like I'm not making progress as quickly as I'd like.
Assistant: It's great that you're using a variety of methods to learn the language. Sometimes, progress can be slow, but it's normal. What do you think is missing from your current routine that's making it hard for you to stay motivated?
User: Hmm, that's a good question. I think I just need to find more interesting ways to practice. I feel like I'm just doing the same old things over and over again.
Assistant: That makes sense. One way to mix things up is to incorporate more authentic materials into your practice, such as books, podcasts, or TV shows in the target language. Have you tried anything like that?
User: Actually, that's something I've been wanting to do, but I'm having a hard time finding access to those kinds of materials.
Assistant: There are many online resources that offer free or low-cost access to authentic language materials. What specific type of material are you interested in? Maybe I can help you find some options.
User: Well, I think it would be great to watch some TV shows or listen to podcasts in the target language. But like I said, I'm having trouble finding access to them.
Assistant: I see. Limited access to authentic materials can definitely make it harder to stay engaged and motivated. Are you in a location where it's difficult to get internet access or is there another reason why you're having trouble finding these materials?
User: Yeah, that's exactly the problem. The person has limited access to authentic language materials, such as books, podcasts, or TV shows, which makes it harder for them to stay engaged and motivated. I mean, I'm that person. User: What are some effective strategies for learning a new language?
Assistant: 1. Immersion: Surround yourself with the language as much as possible. Watch TV shows, movies, and listen to music in the language you are trying to learn.

2. Practice: Regularly practice speaking, writing, reading, and listening in the language. Find a language exchange partner, use language learning apps, and join language learning groups.

3. Goal setting: Set realistic goals for yourself, such as learning a certain number of words or mastering a specific grammar rule each week.

4. Simplify: Start by focusing on the most common words, phrases, and grammar rules that you are likely to use daily. Don't overburden yourself with complex vocabulary or grammar that is not relevant.

5. Patience: Learning a new language takes time, and there will be moments where you feel frustrated or discouraged. Be patient with yourself and celebrate the small successes along the way.

6. Consistency: Consistency is key when learning a language. Make a daily or weekly schedule for language learning and stick to it.

7. Cultural understanding: Learn about the culture of the language you are trying to learn to better understand the language and enhance your communication with native speakers.

8. Use Real-life scenarios: Practice using the language in real-life scenarios, such as ordering food in a restaurant, asking for directions, or introducing yourself to native speakers.

User: What are some effective strategies for learning a new language?
Assistant: 1. Immersion: Surround yourself with the language as much as possible. Watch TV shows, movies, and listen to music in the language you are trying to learn.

2. Practice: Regularly practice speaking, writing, reading, and listening in the language. Find a language exchange partner, use language learning apps, and join language learning groups.

3. Goal setting: Set realistic goals for yourself, such as learning a certain number of words or mastering a specific grammar rule each week.

4. Simplify: Start by focusing on the most common words, phrases, and grammar rules that you are likely to use daily. Don't overburden yourself with complex vocabulary or grammar that is not relevant.

5. Patience: Learning a new language takes time, and there will be moments where you feel frustrated or discouraged. Be patient with yourself and celebrate the small successes along the way.

6. Consistency: Consistency is key when learning a language. Make a daily or weekly schedule for language learning and stick to it.

7. Cultural understanding: Learn about the culture of the language you are trying to learn to better understand the language and enhance your communication with native speakers.

8. Use Real-life scenarios: Practice using the language in real-life scenarios, such as ordering food in a restaurant, asking for directions, or introducing yourself to native speakers.

User: Write an informative essay of at least 600 words, with proper introduction, body and conclusion, exploring the various benefits of learning a new language. Your essay should include concrete examples and statistics to support your claims, and should cover areas such as improved cognitive abilities, enhanced career prospects, cross-cultural communication, and personal growth. The essay must be well-structured and cohesive, with appropriate references to additional sources. Try to engage the reader with interesting and creative examples and analogies, and demonstrate your own passion for language learning through your writing.
Assistant: Language is the most basic form of human communication, and it serves as a gateway to a world of opportunities. Learning a new language is a valuable experience that can have far-reaching benefits. Apart from facilitating cross-cultural communication, language learning can enhance cognitive abilities, provide career opportunities, and promote personal growth.

One of the most significant advantages of learning a new language is the cognitive benefits it provides. Studies have shown that learning a new language can improve cognitive abilities such as memory, concentration, and problem-solving skills. According to Dr. Ellen Bialystok, a professor of psychology at York University, bilingual individuals have better control over their attention and are better at multitasking than monolingual individuals. In addition, learning a new language has been linked to improved memory and delayed onset of age-related cognitive decline.

Moreover, learning a new language can significantly enhance one’s employability prospects. Businesses and organizations often seek out individuals who possess additional language skills, as multilingual employees bring a range of benefits to the workplace. According to a study by the Center for Applied Linguistics, over 200 languages are spoken in the United States. Thus, employers value employees who can communicate with clients, suppliers, and stakeholders in different languages. Furthermore, the ability to communicate with people from different backgrounds and cultures is becoming increasingly important in today’s interconnected world, and language learning can equip individuals with these essential skills.

Another significant benefit of learning a new language is the opportunity it provides for cross-cultural communication. The modern world is highly interconnected, and multilingual individuals have the privilege of being able to communicate with people from different backgrounds, cultures, and ways of thinking. Language fluency helps in understanding and appreciating cultural differences, leading to more profound insights into people's values, behaviors, and beliefs. Moreover, the ability to communicate in different languages can facilitate both personal and business relationships, offer global perspectives, and promote international collaboration.

Furthermore, language learning can promote personal growth by broadening one’s worldview. Learning a new language involves learning about the traditions and culture of the speaker’s native country, which can be highly informative and enjoyable. Moreover, learning a new language can open doors to literature, films, and music that one would not have been exposed to previously. Learning a new language can also challenge one’s cognitive and problem-solving skills, leading to a greater sense of achievement and self-confidence.

In learning a new language, personal motivation is the key driver. Learning a new language is a long-term process that requires persistence, patience, and dedication. However, the benefits of the learning experience provide a significant boost to motivation. One of the most effective ways to learn a new language is through immersion. Immersion involves being immersed in the language, culture, and daily life of the native speakers. This involves living in a foreign country, attending language classes, studying literature, and speaking with native speakers. This provides a comprehensive learning experience that accelerates the learning process.

An integral part of language learning is the process of making mistakes. The fear of making mistakes can be a significant barrier to language learning. However, making mistakes is an essential part of the learning process, and one should not be afraid of making them. Mistakes provide an opportunity for feedback and learning, leading to greater proficiency in the language.

In conclusion, learning a new language is a valuable experience that offers a wealth of benefits, including enhanced cognitive abilities, heightened employability prospects, cross-cultural communication skills, and personal growth. Learning a language is a challenging process that demands commitment, persistence, and dedication. However, the benefits of learning a new language make it a worthwhile investment of time and effort. When individuals learn a new language, they gain new skills and insights that contribute to their personal and professional development.
User: Thank you for the informative essay on the benefits of learning a new language. Can you please provide me with some additional information on how language learning can improve memory and delay cognitive decline? I would also appreciate it if you could provide me with some tips on how to accelerate the language learning process through immersion.
Assistant: Certainly, I'll be happy to provide more information on these topics.

Research has demonstrated that the process of language learning can improve memory and delay cognitive decline. Learning a new language requires the use of the brain's working memory, which is responsible for holding information in the short term while performing mental tasks. As language learners acquire vocabulary, syntax, and grammar, they are essentially working out their brain and building new neural connections. This process can lead to better cognitive abilities and improved memory as the brain's capacity to store and retrieve information expands.

In addition to enhancing cognitive abilities, language learning has been shown to delay the onset of age-related cognitive decline. According to a study published in the Annals of Neurology, bilingual individuals showed signs of dementia an average of 4.5 years later than monolingual individuals. The study suggests that bilingualism improves cognitive reserve, which is the brain's ability to cope with age-related cognitive decline.

When it comes to accelerating the language learning process, immersion is one of the most effective methods. Immersion involves being surrounded by the language and culture of native speakers, which helps learners develop fluency more quickly. Here are some tips for using immersion to accelerate language learning:

1. Find language exchange partners: Partnering with a native speaker who wants to learn your native language can be a great way to immerse yourself in the language. Language exchange partners can help with conversation practice and provide insight into the culture and idiomatic expressions.

2. Attend language courses: Language courses offered at language schools are often immersive and involve classes, cultural activities, and excursions. Attending language courses provides an ideal opportunity to practice the language with other learners and native speakers.

3. Watch TV shows and movies in the target language: Watching TV shows and movies is a fun way to immerse yourself in the language. It can also help you become familiar with everyday expressions and intonations used by native speakers.

4. Travel to a country where the target language is spoken: Traveling to a country where the target language is spoken offers an excellent opportunity to immerse yourself in the language and culture. You will be able to observe and interact with native speakers in real-life situations, which can be highly beneficial in accelerating the language learning process.

In conclusion, language learning offers a wide range of benefits, from enhancing cognitive abilities to improving employability prospects and promoting personal growth. Immersion is a highly effective method of accelerating language learning, and there are numerous ways to immerse oneself in the language, including language exchange, language courses, TV shows and movies, and travel. With determination, persistence, and immersion, learners can experience the joys and benefits of language acquisition.

User: How does The Wind Rises compare to Miyazaki's previous works in terms of subject matter and visual beauty? Answer according to: On the same day that the 72-year-old Japanese legend announced his retirement, festivalgoers clammored to catch his new animated biopic of Jiro Horikoshi.
TELLURIDE, Colo. -- Mere hours after the Japanese anime master Hayao Miyazaki announced his retirement, I caught the first North American screening of what will be his last film, The Wind Rises, an animated biopic of Jiro Horikoshi, the aeronautical engineer who designed the fighter planes that Japan used in World War II while the love of his life was dying. The film, which premiered in Venice earlier in the day and will be released stateside by Disney's Touchstone Pictures later this year, screened at the Chuck Jones Cinema, appropriately enough.
The Wind Rises deals with darker subject matter than the 10 earlier films for which the 72-year-old filmmaker is internationally known -- including Princess Mononoke (1997), the Oscar-winning Spirited Away (2001), Howl's Moving Castle (2004) and Ponyo (2008) -- but it is as visually beautiful as any of them. On the basis of its quality, Miyazaki's big announcement and the relatively weak animated competition this year, I strongly suspect that the film will be nominated for the best animated feature Oscar.
The film unfolds in 1920s and 1930s Japan, as Horikoshi, who as a child dreamed of building aircrafts, struggles to bring Japanese aviation into the modern age. Frustrated at the engineering prowess, or lack thereof, of his "poor and backward" country, he seeks information and inspiration from every source imaginable (i.e. The Germans) -- and some purely imagined (i.e. An Italian engineer named Carboni pops up in numerous dream sequences).
In fact, what is and isn't real in the film sometimes becomes a bit blurry, but what never wavers is Horikoshi's Miyazaki-like vision and commitment: he just wants to make something beautiful, through whatever means necessary. He's not particularly patriotic; the fact that his creation will be used in the cause of war -- such as in the Dec. 7, 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor -- is not something that is even very much on his mind.
There are certain sequences in the film that are particularly striking to behold: a massive earthquake, a big rain storm, shadows of people running down an alley, a plane catching fire and crashing from the sky -- and the list goes on. But the film also has undeniable flaws: it features all sorts of unnecessary repetition and meandering, which push its runtime to 126 minutes, way too long for a relatively simple story.
Power-producers Kathleen Kennedy and Frank Marshall, friends of "Miyazaki-san" who have helped his films secure better North American distribution in recent years, introduced The Wind Rises. Kennedy said that a Horkioshi film has been on the director's to-do list for years, and that he even considered making it as a live-action film. She also noted Miyazaki's retirement announcement -- which was met with gasps from many audience members who hadn't heard the news -- and Marshall added, "In our opinion, he saved his best for last."
Follow Scott on Twitter @ScottFeinberg for additional news and analysis.

User: Could you please summarize the plot of Howl’s Moving Castle and compare it with Miyazaki’s other movie plots?: Two years ago, Spirited Away won an Academy Award for Best Animated Picture. For many Americans, it was their first taste of the fantastic world of Hayao Miyazaki (and if you haven’t seen his other films, get thee to the Video Station).
Miyazaki follows it up with another magical movie with a strong young heroine named Sophie (voiced by both Emily Mortimer and Jean Simmons in the dubbed American release). She makes hats in a nameless, quaint, post-Victorian village. She encounters a hunk of a young man in an alley who is trying to escape from some oil-blob baddies who materialize out of the walls. Sophie seems as surprised by their appearance as we are, although that’s not half as surprising as when the boy flies her home to her balcony.
Soon thereafter, an enormous witch with six or seven chins visits Sophie and casts a spell on her, turning her into an old woman and forbidding her to speak of the spell. Who are these people? Why are they picking on a poor hatmaker? And who is this Howl person that the witch mentioned? We’d like to know, too.
A turnip-headed scarecrow helps her find the way to a gigantic walking castle. Inside, she befriends a fire demon named Calcifer (Billy Crystal, who is grating until you acclimate to his voice), a boy apprentice named Markl (Josh Hutcherson), and a familiar-looking wizard named Howl (Christian Bale).
At two hours long, the movie covers a lot of ground, but the plot boils down to this: many different people need to undo curses and spells that keep them from being their true selves.
Visually, Howl’s Moving Castle is as good as any other Miyazaki movie. The world looks like Alaska in summertime. There are green grassy wetlands sprinkled liberally with small wildflowers and clear, cool daylight. The characters, too, are animated with all the love and attention needed to bring them to life.
The plot, however, doesn’t seem as compelling as Sen’s rescue of her parents in Spirited Away or of the restoration of the forest in Princess Mononoke. Lifting spells and breaking curses seems pretty abstract, and feels more like a contrivance than some of Miyazaki’s other movie’s plots. It also lends itself to some anti-climactic climaxes.
The DVD comes with the usual batch of extras that Disney has put on its other Miyazaki releases. It has Behind the Microphone, with interviews of the English-dub cast and crew. It has some featurettes about the movie made for Japanese TV. And disc two is reserved for a storyboards-only version of the movie.
The Japanese TV segments, called Interview with Pete Docter and Hello Mr. Lasseter, are definitely worth a look. They can be a bit confusing because the questions are asked in Japanese (with no translation) and the answers are presented in English. But both Docter and Lasseter have the usual upbeat stories to tell about the production and the redub of the movie for American audiences.
The first part of Hello Mr. Lasseter features video footage of Miyazaki’s surprise visit to Pixar HQ and John Lasseter’s excited, surprised welcome. Miyazaki had brought a giant stuffed cat bus (from My Neighbor Totoro), which he presented to Lasseter.
The DVD also a section of TV spots and trailers from Japan that didn’t do much for me.
In my theatrical review I said that no home video version could do justice to the detail packed into the screen at theaters. And although I have a pretty big screen at home, I have to say that I was less taken by the detail on DVD than I was in the theater.
That said, the DVD looks as good as can be expected. The colors are rich and striking, and the print is pristine. The audio is recorded in Dolby Digital 5.1 in English, Japanese, and French tracks.

This Japanese-U.S. Coproduction is a fun animated fantasy adventure, which keeps at least some of the iconography of McKay's comic. It does take lots of liberties, and I'm not sure the dark nightmare villain comes from the comics. It would be hard to match the level of surrealism and raw weirdness that McKay packed into every page of his comic, and the animated film instead settles for a kind of gentle Seussian strangeness, which meshes pretty well with the whole "dreamland" aesthetic.

Passage: Winsor McKay didn't just create one of the most influential comics of all time, Little Nemo in Slumberland — he also was an animation pioneer, creating some of the first real animated films. So it's kind of sad that the animated movie version of Little Nemo, from 1992, was such a flop — at one point, I saw it listed as the most unsuccessful comic-book adaptation ever released in theaters. But at the moment, it's being beaten by Dylan Dog: Dead of Night and Return of the Swamp Thing.
In any case, Little Nemo: Adventures in Slumberland is actually not a terrible film. According to one IMDB review, Hiyao Miyazaki, Moebius and Brian Froud all worked on it, which is a major plus. This Japanese-U.S. Coproduction is a fun animated fantasy adventure, which keeps at least some of the iconography of McKay's comic. It does take lots of liberties, and I'm not sure the dark nightmare villain comes from the comics. It would be hard to match the level of surrealism and raw weirdness that McKay packed into every page of his comic, and the animated film instead settles for a kind of gentle Seussian strangeness, which meshes pretty well with the whole "dreamland" aesthetic.
Assistant: Winsor McKay contributed to the field of animation by creating some of the first real animated films. He was an animation pioneer.
User: Can you provide me with some more information about Winsor McKay's contributions to animation?
Assistant: Sure, Winsor McCay was an American cartoonist, animator, and vaudeville performer who was widely regarded as a pioneer in the field of animation. In 1905, he began creating short animated films using his characters, such as "Little Nemo" and "Gertie the Dinosaur." His films were notable for their technical innovation and attention to detail, and helped to establish animation as a legitimate art form. In addition to his work in animation, McCay was also a celebrated newspaper cartoonist, creating comic strips such as "Little Nemo in Slumberland" and "Dream of the Rarebit Fiend." His influence can be seen in the work of many of today's animators and cartoonists.

I would like to think that Asimov would like this movie. However, look at what happened to Robert A. Heinlein on "Destination Moon".

I will even go so far as to say it was much better than the Afro Samurai anime. From the direction to the final editing, this film is a classic to watch over and over again. I recommend watching this in its original Japanese or dubbed German with English subtitles."
User: Oh, I've already seen "Vampire Hunter D VHS", so I'll pass. Do you have any other recommendations?
Assistant: No problem! How about "April and the Extraordinary World"? It's a visually stunning French animated movie set in an alternate timeline where steam power is prevalent.
